nga-166436: In 1857, a young American painter put Niagara Falls on a canvas more than two metres wide, and somehow made people feel they were about to tip over the edge. There's no riverbank and no railing, just green water racing towards the drop and a faint rainbow hanging in the mist.

Church showed this single painting on its own in a New York gallery, and thousands of people paid to see it within weeks. It then toured to London, where critics were just as stunned. Most people back then would never travel to Niagara, so this was the closest they'd get to the roar. Leaving out the shoreline was the trick: it turns a view into a free fall.

This belongs to the Hudson River School, America's first homegrown landscape movement. It was started by Thomas Cole in the 1820s, who painted the wild Catskill Mountains as almost sacred places. Fun fact: the name only came later, and was reportedly meant as a put-down. Painters like Church and Albert Bierstadt turned huge landscapes into ticketed events, a bit like blockbuster films.

Frederic Edwin Church, born in 1826, was Cole's only formal student. He chased extremes, from volcanoes in the Andes to icebergs off Labrador, and later built a fantasy house called Olana high above the Hudson. His whole career was about one feeling: how small you are next to something enormous.
nga-46: This is the moment the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will have a son. Gabriel is dressed in red and gold, with wings that melt from blue into crimson. Mary kneels in blue. Golden words float between them, and hers are painted upside down.

Gabriel says, 'Hail, full of grace.' Mary answers, 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord,' and her words are upside down so heaven can read them. The scene is set inside a church: heavy rounded arches below and lighter windows above, which may suggest the old world turning into a new one. The painting once hung in the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg, until the Soviet government sold it around 1930 to the American collector Andrew Mellon, whose gift helped found the National Gallery of Art.

This is Early Netherlandish painting, from the 1400s in cities like Bruges and Ghent. These artists layered thin, glassy coats of oil paint to make jewels, metal and skin glow. Fun fact: the Renaissance writer Vasari claimed van Eyck invented oil painting. He didn't, but he perfected it. Everyday objects often carried hidden meanings, like the lilies here, a symbol of purity.

Jan van Eyck was court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy. He even went on secret diplomatic missions, including a trip to Portugal to paint the duke's future bride. He signed his work with a motto, 'as I can', a humble joke from someone who could do almost anything with paint.
nga-1138: A woodland picnic of the gods: nymphs, satyrs and gods lounging, pouring wine and eating fruit. It looks peaceful, but it's actually the setup for a very old joke, and two of the greatest painters of Venice both had a hand in it.

The joke comes from the Roman poet Ovid. At a feast, the god Priapus creeps towards a sleeping nymph called Lotis, but a donkey brays, everyone wakes up, and he's laughed out of the party. The Duke of Ferrara, Alfonso d'Este, commissioned it for a private room of paintings. Bellini signed it in 1514, in his eighties. After he died, Titian repainted the landscape and added the big rocky hill, probably to match his own pictures for the room. X-rays show both layers.

This is Venetian Renaissance painting. Florence prized drawing, but Venice prized colour. Its damp sea air was hard on frescoes, so Venetians took to oil on canvas early. Fun fact: the blue-and-white bowls in this picture are Chinese porcelain, among the earliest shown in a European painting, a sign of Venice's global trade.

Giovanni Bellini led Venetian painting for half a century, and he died in 1516. Titian trained in his circle. When the German artist Albrecht Dürer visited Venice in 1506, he wrote that Bellini was very old but still the best painter in the city.
nga-43626: This face is about eighteen hundred years old, and it still looks like it could speak. A young woman with huge dark eyes, red-and-white earrings and a purple garment trimmed with gold, painted on a thin panel of wood.

It was painted in Egypt when Egypt was part of the Roman Empire. Portraits like this were made to be wrapped into a mummy's linen bandages, right over the face, so the person would be recognised in the afterlife. That's why the faces are so direct. They weren't decoration. They were the person, looking out forever.

These are often called Fayum portraits, after the oasis south of Cairo where many were found in the late 1800s. Around a thousand survive. They mix Egyptian burial customs with Greek and Roman painting. Fun fact: they're painted in encaustic, pigment mixed into hot beeswax, which is why the colours still glow. Experts date them by their hairstyles and jewellery, which followed Roman fashion.

We don't know who painted her, or her name. Skilled workshops made these portraits, and they're among the oldest realistic painted portraits to survive anywhere. She's a reminder that the ancient world was full of real, specific people.
nga-231465: A woman sits in darkness, head tipped back, eyes closed, hands wrapped around her knees, with light falling across her face. She isn't posing for anyone. She's completely somewhere else.

Mary Magdalene was a follower of Jesus. Later legends said she spent years praying in the wilderness, overwhelmed by visions. In the 1600s the Catholic Church encouraged images of deep personal faith and repentance, and the Magdalene became one of the most popular subjects around. Artemisia gives her real weight and a lived-in body, so it reads as an inner experience rather than a pretty pose.

This style is called Caravaggism, after Caravaggio, who caused a sensation in Rome around 1600 with figures picked out of pitch darkness by a spotlight. Italians called it tenebrism, from the word for darkness. Within a few years painters across Europe were copying it. Artemisia's father, Orazio, knew Caravaggio personally.

Artemisia Gentileschi was born in Rome in 1593. She became the first woman admitted to the Academy of Design in Florence, worked for the Medici, and later joined her father at the court of King Charles the First in London. She was famous for painting strong, decisive women, and today she's one of the best-loved painters of her century.
nga-121096: At first it's just curving lines and colour, blue, yellow and pink, bending like branches. Then two small red creatures appear: one up a tree, one on the ground looking up. Those are the weasels, almost melting into the forest.

Marc painted this in 1911, the year everything changed for him. He believed animals lived in harmony with nature in a way people had lost, so he painted them instead of humans. He also gave colours meanings: blue for the spiritual, yellow for gentleness and joy, and red for heavy, earthly matter.

This is German Expressionism, and specifically the Blue Rider group, which Marc founded in Munich in 1911 with Wassily Kandinsky. Fun fact: Kandinsky later said the name came from their shared love of blue, Marc's love of horses and his own love of riders. Their 1912 almanac mixed paintings with folk art, children's drawings and music, which was radical for its time.

Franz Marc was born in Munich in 1880. His blue horses and yellow cows became icons of modern art. He was killed at the Battle of Verdun in 1916, aged just 36. In five short years he showed how colour alone can carry a feeling.
nga-61253: A wall of giant leaves in every shade of green, spiky orange flowers, and five monkeys climbing, swinging and sitting. The big brown one at the bottom stares straight out of the picture. It's a jungle, painted by a man who never saw one.

Rousseau painted this in 1910, the year he died. He never left France. He built his jungles from visits to the Paris botanical gardens and zoo, from illustrated books and from his imagination. For years critics laughed at his flat, careful style. Then the younger avant-garde decided he was a genius.

This is called naive art: work by self-taught painters who ignore the academic rules, and Rousseau is its most famous example. Fun fact: in 1908 Picasso threw him a famous banquet in his studio. Rousseau reportedly told Picasso they were the two greatest painters of the age, Picasso in the Egyptian style and himself in the modern style.

Henri Rousseau, born in 1844, worked as a toll collector on the edge of Paris, so he was nicknamed Le Douanier, the customs man. He only painted full-time after he retired, in his late forties. He's proof that you don't need permission, or a passport, to make something the world remembers.
nga-50215: Two aristocratic friends share a garden bench at dusk. One looks straight out at us, and the other has her arm around her son, while the younger boy rests his head in her lap. Everyone is touching and half-smiling. For a portrait of French nobility in 1787, that's surprisingly cosy.

This was painted two years before the French Revolution swept this world away. Formal portraits of the nobility were usually stiff and grand. But a new fashion for warmth, natural motherhood and feeling was spreading, and Vigée Le Brun was its star. The shimmering blue-pink dress shows off her skill with fabric.

This is 18th-century French portraiture at the moment it softened. Fun fact: in the same year, 1787, Vigée Le Brun showed a self-portrait smiling with her lips parted and her teeth just visible. It caused a scandal at the Paris Salon, because a smile with teeth was considered improper in serious art.

Élisabeth Louise Vigée Le Brun, born in Paris in 1755, was largely self-taught and became Marie Antoinette's favourite portraitist. When the Revolution came she fled, spent twelve years painting royalty from Naples to Saint Petersburg, and painted around six hundred and sixty portraits in her career. She later wrote a lively memoir.
nga-51140: A wide outdoor scene in 19th-century China. An archer in red draws his bow at a row of targets, while officials watch from a pavilion under a carved canopy. Horses are tied to a fence, and colourful flags fly over white tents in the distance.

China was ruled by the Qing dynasty, whose emperors were Manchu. For the Manchus, archery and horsemanship were part of who they were, and military examinations tested skill with the bow. So a contest like this was serious public business, judged by officials. The long braids are the queue hairstyle that men under the Qing were required to wear.

It's painted in oil on cotton, which is unusual for China, so it may be a China trade painting. In the 1700s and 1800s, workshops in Canton made pictures of Chinese life in Western techniques for foreign merchants. Fun fact: for about eighty years Canton was the only Chinese port where Western traders were allowed to do business, so these paintings were many Europeans' main picture of China.

We don't know the painter's name. Trade paintings were usually made in busy workshops, with different hands doing figures, buildings and landscape. What survives is a sharp eye for ceremony, costume and crowds, and a window onto a world on the edge of huge change.
nga-56101: A tabletop seen from above, broken into pieces: a newspaper that reads Le Journal, a pipe, a checkerboard and a green booklet with the word Fantômas and a black mask. Nothing quite lines up. Wood grain cuts through the letters, and a goblet floats on top in white outline.

Fantômas was a master criminal from a wildly popular series of French crime novels that began in 1911, and then from silent films. The Paris avant-garde adored him, and the poet Guillaume Apollinaire even founded a fan club. Gris painted this in August 1915, in wartime Paris, slipping pop culture into a serious still life.

This is Cubism, invented around 1907 to 1908 by Picasso and Georges Braque, who showed objects from several angles at once. The name came from a critic mocking their 'little cubes'. Fun fact: Braque had trained as a house painter, which is where the fake wood grain came from. That's a decorator's trick, turned into fine art.

Juan Gris was born in Madrid in 1887 and moved to Paris at nineteen, living in the same ramshackle studio building as Picasso. He became the clearest and most elegant of the Cubists. He died in 1927, aged only forty, and left behind some of the calmest pictures of a chaotic movement.
